notes: Replaced policy-simulator-production-effects with policy-simulator-service-condition-key-support to avoid a name giveaway. Replaced access-analyzer-finding-versus-use with access-analyzer-organization-zone-of-trust to avoid repeating the earlier static-analysis-versus-observed-use distractor. Replaced emr-inter-node-encryption-security-configuration with emr-application-overrides-transport-gap to test an enforcement gap rather than a setting name. Replaced identity-center-permission-set-reprovision with saml-encrypted-assertion-provider-endpoint to keep section 4.1 focused on authentication rather than routine authorization provisioning.

cards.statement: IAM compares a SAML assertion's Recipient with the role's SAML:aud trust condition during console federation.
cards.explanation: An IAM role's SAML:aud trust condition evaluates the assertion's Recipient value. Matching it to the approved AWS sign-in endpoint restricts where console federation completes.

source.title: Create a role for SAML 2.0 federation (console)

cards.statement: IAM can validate an OIDC JWKS endpoint's TLS certificate through its trusted root CA library.
cards.explanation: IAM normally checks the JWKS endpoint against trusted root CAs. Configured thumbprints remain a fallback, such as when the endpoint's CA is outside that library.

source.title: Obtain the thumbprint for an OpenID Connect identity provider

cards.statement: Enabling console MFA automatically protects an IAM user's API calls made with their long-term access keys.
cards.explanation: Console MFA does not impose an MFA check on long-term access keys. Administrators enforce MFA for API access through policies and MFA-authenticated temporary credentials.
cards.misconception: Enabling an IAM user's console MFA also enforces MFA for API requests signed with their long-term access keys.

source.title: Secure API access with MFA

cards.statement: An STS session's expiration limits the lifetime of an Amazon S3 presigned URL signed with its credentials.
cards.explanation: An Amazon S3 presigned URL signed with temporary credentials expires when those credentials expire, even if its requested expiration time is later.

source.title: Download and upload objects with presigned URLs

cards.statement: Amazon S3 consumes a presigned URL after the first successful use of its authorized operation.
cards.explanation: Amazon S3 presigned URLs permit repeated use while valid. A successful authorized request does not consume the URL.
cards.misconception: An Amazon S3 presigned URL is a single-use authorization token.

source.title: Download and upload objects with presigned URLs

cards.statement: AWS IAM Identity Center revokes AWS account role sessions when a user signs out of the AWS access portal.
cards.explanation: Signing out of the AWS access portal ends the sign-in session. Existing AWS account role sessions continue until their configured expiration.
cards.misconception: Signing out of the AWS access portal revokes temporary credentials already issued for AWS account roles.

source.title: Understanding authentication sessions in IAM Identity Center

cards.statement: AWS requires the IAM SAML provider's unique identifier in the sign-in URL for encrypted console federation.
cards.explanation: For encrypted SAML console assertions, the AWS sign-in URL includes /saml/acs/<IdP-ID>. Engineers obtain this identifier from the IAM SAML provider's details page.

source.title: Create a role for SAML 2.0 federation (console)

cards.statement: IAM rejects a SAML assertion when the signing certificate in its uploaded IdP metadata has expired.
cards.explanation: IAM ignores the expiration of an uploaded SAML signing certificate during authentication. It evaluates the assertion's NotOnOrAfter conditions instead.
cards.misconception: IAM treats expiration of the identity provider's uploaded signing certificate as a federation authentication failure.

source.title: Create a SAML identity provider in IAM

cards.statement: An IAM role session can obtain MFA-authenticated credentials by calling GetSessionToken with its existing credentials.
cards.explanation: GetSessionToken requires long-term credentials from an IAM user or the account root user. Temporary credentials from an assumed role are ineligible.
cards.misconception: An assumed role's temporary credentials are an eligible caller for GetSessionToken.

source.title: GetSessionToken

cards.statement: STS returns an IAM role session's identity despite an identity policy's explicit Deny of GetCallerIdentity.
cards.explanation: STS returns the caller's identity even when an identity policy denies GetCallerIdentity. This makes the API useful for identifying the credentials involved in an authorization failure.

source.title: GetCallerIdentity

cards.statement: Amazon EC2 rejects an IMDSv2 token when a caller uses it to query metadata on a different instance.
cards.explanation: An IMDSv2 token is bound to the instance that creates it. Copying the token to another instance does not authorize metadata requests there.

source.title: Use the Instance Metadata Service to access instance metadata

cards.statement: Amazon Cognito's token revocation makes an unexpired access token fail offline JWT signature validation.
cards.explanation: Revoked, unexpired Amazon Cognito tokens still pass local signature and expiration checks. Cognito's authenticated APIs enforce revocation; those local checks do not query revocation state.
cards.misconception: Cryptographic signature and expiration validation reveal Amazon Cognito's token revocation status.

source.title: Ending user sessions with token revocation

cards.statement: During IAM authorization, a session tag takes precedence over a role tag with the same key.
cards.explanation: AWS STS gives a passed session tag precedence over a matching role tag. An aws:PrincipalTag condition therefore sees the session's value.

source.title: AssumeRole

cards.statement: An implicit boundary deny limits a same-account resource policy's grant directly to an IAM role session ARN.
cards.explanation: A same-account resource policy grant directly to a role session ARN bypasses implicit denies in the permissions boundary. Explicit denies still apply.
cards.misconception: A permissions boundary's implicit deny restricts a same-account resource policy grant directly to a role session ARN.

source.title: Permissions boundaries for IAM entities

cards.statement: A NotPrincipal Deny can directly block a same-account IAM role with a boundary even when the exception names that role.
cards.explanation: NotPrincipal with Deny blocks IAM principals that have permissions boundaries even when listed as exceptions. AWS recommends ArnNotEquals with aws:PrincipalArn for this restriction.

source.title: Permissions boundaries for IAM entities

cards.statement: An IAM user's cross-account AssumeRole requires an identity policy Allow and the target role's trust policy Allow.
cards.explanation: Cross-account role assumption needs the caller's identity permissions and trust from the destination role. Authorization from one account alone is insufficient.

source.title: Cross-account policy evaluation logic

cards.statement: An AssumeRole session policy can grant an action beyond the role's identity policy permissions.
cards.explanation: A session policy restricts the permissions granted by the role's identity policies. Adding an action to the session policy does not expand that grant.
cards.misconception: A session policy supplements the role's identity policy permissions with additional actions.

source.title: AssumeRole

cards.statement: An IAM user switching to a same-account role automatically adds their user permissions to the role session.
cards.explanation: Switching to an IAM role sets aside the user's permissions while the role is active. The role session's permissions do not accumulate the user's permissions.
cards.misconception: Assuming a role combines the IAM user's existing permissions with the role's permissions.

source.title: Switch from a user to an IAM role (console)

cards.statement: A Step Functions role trust policy can use aws:SourceArn to restrict assumption to a specified state machine.
cards.explanation: Matching the state machine's ARN in aws:SourceArn binds Step Functions' role assumption to the approved source resource, reducing cross-service confused deputy risk.

source.title: Creating an IAM role for your state machine in Step Functions

cards.statement: AWS recommends that a customer choose the ExternalId its third-party provider uses for AssumeRole.
cards.explanation: AWS recommends that the third-party provider generate a unique external ID for each customer. Provider control of that mapping prevents customers from choosing another customer's ID.
cards.misconception: The trusting customer should generate the external ID for a third-party provider's multi-customer role access.

source.title: Access to AWS accounts owned by third parties

cards.statement: IAM Roles Anywhere can map X.509 certificate attributes into principal tags for authorization.
cards.explanation: An IAM Roles Anywhere profile's attribute mappings select which certificate values become principal tags. IAM policy conditions use those values to restrict the resulting role session.

source.title: Attribute mapping and trust policy

cards.statement: An organization-scoped IAM Access Analyzer can flag a resource grant to another member account as external access.
cards.explanation: An organization-scoped IAM Access Analyzer includes the organization's member accounts in its zone of trust. Resource-policy grants to those accounts stay inside that boundary.
cards.misconception: An organization-scoped external access analyzer treats cross-account grants inside the organization as external access.

source.title: Using AWS Identity and Access Management Access Analyzer

cards.statement: The IAM policy simulator can verify service support for global condition keys in an identity-based policy.
cards.explanation: For identity-based policies, the simulator evaluates supplied condition values but does not establish whether a service supports the global condition key. Validate service support separately.
cards.misconception: A successful IAM simulation verifies that the target service supports the policy's global condition keys.
cards.volatilityNote: AWS may expand the simulator's service-aware validation of global condition keys.

source.title: IAM policy testing with the IAM policy simulator

cards.statement: Amazon Verified Permissions denies access when a matching forbid policy conflicts with a matching permit policy.
cards.explanation: When both policy effects match an authorization request, the forbid policy determines Amazon Verified Permissions' Deny decision.

source.title: IsAuthorized

cards.statement: An Application Load Balancer can reject an HTTPS target specifically because its server certificate has expired.
cards.explanation: An Application Load Balancer establishes TLS to HTTPS targets but skips validation of their server certificates. An expired target certificate alone does not prevent that connection.
cards.misconception: HTTPS target connections include server-certificate expiration validation by the load balancer.

source.title: Target groups for your Application Load Balancers

cards.statement: AWS PrivateLink enables TLS for a plaintext TCP application by default when engineers create an interface endpoint.
cards.explanation: AWS PrivateLink provides a private network path rather than adding TLS to a plaintext application. Engineers configure transport encryption in the application or its supporting infrastructure.
cards.misconception: Creating a private endpoint supplies application TLS encryption automatically.

source.title: AWS PrivateLink FAQs

cards.statement: A CloudWatch interface endpoint with private DNS disabled maps the Regional service hostname to endpoint IPs.
cards.explanation: A CloudWatch interface endpoint maps the default Regional service hostname to endpoint IPs through enabled private DNS. Disabling that setting leaves endpoint-specific DNS names available.
cards.misconception: An interface endpoint redirects the ordinary service hostname even with private DNS disabled.

source.title: Access AWS services through AWS PrivateLink

cards.statement: Amazon S3 can supply the client's private IP as aws:SourceIp for requests through an S3 gateway endpoint.
cards.explanation: For S3 requests through a VPC endpoint, aws:SourceIp is unavailable for bucket or identity policy conditions. Use aws:VpcSourceIp to evaluate the client's private IP address.
cards.misconception: The ordinary source-IP condition key carries the private client address through an S3 gateway endpoint.

source.title: Gateway endpoints for Amazon S3

cards.statement: By default, eligible EC2 instances preserve Nitro instance-to-instance encryption across a middlebox path.
cards.explanation: EC2's default Nitro instance-to-instance encryption excludes paths through virtual network devices. That default guarantee does not cover traffic routed through a middlebox.
cards.misconception: The automatic encryption between eligible EC2 instances extends through an intermediate virtual network device.

source.title: Data protection in Amazon EC2

cards.statement: AWS Verified Access reuses initial HTTP authorization for later requests in the same TCP connection.
cards.explanation: AWS Verified Access evaluates each HTTP application request against its access requirements. A prior authorized request does not replace assessment of the next request.
cards.misconception: Verified Access grants HTTP access for an entire TCP connection after the first authorization decision.

source.title: What is AWS Verified Access?

cards.statement: An S3 bucket policy with Principal "*" can enforce HTTPS for anonymous object requests using aws:SecureTransport.
cards.explanation: An S3 bucket policy Deny with Principal "*" and aws:SecureTransport=false applies to anonymous HTTP requests, including access otherwise permitted by a public read grant.

source.title: Examples of Amazon S3 bucket policies

cards.statement: An S3 TLS Deny that requires aws:PrincipalIsAWSService=false exempts AWS service principals from its scope.
cards.explanation: AWS can redact transport context on service-to-service calls. Adding aws:PrincipalIsAWSService=false to a transport Deny excludes AWS service principals from that restriction.

source.title: Bucket policy examples using condition keys

cards.statement: An S3 bucket policy denying s3:* to Principal "*" outside a gateway endpoint blocks console access to that bucket.
cards.explanation: A bucket policy Deny for requests outside an S3 gateway endpoint also rejects public console access. Those console requests carry no matching S3 endpoint ID.

source.title: Controlling access from VPC endpoints with bucket policies

cards.statement: A Network Load Balancer's TCP listener passes TLS through, so the target presents its server certificate.
cards.explanation: A Network Load Balancer passes TLS traffic through its TCP listener unchanged. The target handles the TLS connection and server certificate.

source.title: Listeners for your Network Load Balancers

cards.statement: Amazon EMR application overrides can disable endpoint encryption despite automatically configured transport protection.
cards.explanation: EMR security configurations set application encryption defaults. Application overrides can disable encryption for specific endpoints, so the cluster setting alone does not prove their transport protection.

source.title: Encryption options for Amazon EMR

cards.statement: The Amazon EFS mount helper can use a localhost NFS mount while automatically protecting remote traffic with TLS.
cards.explanation: For a TLS-enabled EFS mount, NFS connects to a local port. The mount helper maintains the encrypted connection from that port to the file system.

source.title: Encrypting data in transit

cards.statement: Engineers can enable S3 Object Lock on an existing versioned Amazon S3 general purpose bucket.
cards.explanation: Object Lock can be activated after an Amazon S3 general purpose bucket exists. The bucket needs versioning enabled before engineers apply object retention controls.

source.title: Configuring S3 Object Lock

cards.statement: Amazon S3 infers a governance bypass request from the caller's s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission.
cards.explanation: Governance bypass needs both s3:BypassGovernanceRetention authorization and the x-amz-bypass-governance-retention:true request header. Permission alone does not express the caller's intent.
cards.misconception: Possessing governance bypass permission automatically requests bypass for a retained version.

source.title: Object Lock considerations

cards.statement: Amazon S3 rejects a root user's DeleteObject request naming a version ID with active compliance retention.
cards.explanation: Compliance-mode S3 Object Lock protects an individual object version against deletion requests even from the account root user until its retention expires.

source.title: Locking objects with Object Lock

cards.statement: Amazon S3 releases a version's legal hold automatically when that version's retention period expires.
cards.explanation: An Amazon S3 legal hold stays active until an authorized caller removes it, even after the version's retention period expires.
cards.misconception: A legal hold shares the expiration date of the object's retention period.

source.title: Locking objects with Object Lock

cards.statement: AWS Backup rejects lock changes on a populated compliance-mode vault after its grace period expires.
cards.explanation: After its compliance-mode grace period, a populated AWS Backup vault's lock configuration is immutable even to AWS. The protection persists while the vault holds recovery points.

source.title: AWS Backup Vault Lock

cards.statement: Amazon S3 requires an explicit replication-rule opt-in before it replicates eligible SSE-KMS-encrypted objects.
cards.explanation: An Amazon S3 replication rule opts in to KMS-encrypted objects through SourceSelectionCriteria. Selecting the bucket's objects alone leaves those encrypted objects outside replication.

source.title: Replicating encrypted objects (SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, DSSE-KMS, SSE-C)

cards.statement: For an SSE-C-enabled bucket, Amazon S3 can retain the supplied encryption key for later object retrieval.
cards.explanation: Amazon S3 discards the SSE-C encryption key after processing the request. The reader provides the key again to decrypt and retrieve the object.
cards.misconception: Amazon S3 preserves customer-provided encryption keys so readers can retrieve encrypted objects later.

source.title: Using server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C)

cards.statement: Engineers can copy an encrypted Amazon EBS snapshot under a different AWS KMS key to replace its key dependency.
cards.explanation: Copying an encrypted Amazon EBS snapshot reencrypts the copy under the selected AWS KMS key. Choosing a recipient-owned key removes the copy's dependence on a snapshot sharer's key.

source.title: Copy an Amazon EBS snapshot

cards.statement: With pre and post scripts disabled, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager pauses database I/O before snapshots.
cards.explanation: Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager defaults to crash-consistent snapshots. Application-consistent backups need appropriate pre and post scripts to freeze, flush and resume workload I/O.
cards.misconception: A Data Lifecycle Manager schedule automatically quiesces database activity for snapshot creation.

source.title: Automate application-consistent snapshots with Data Lifecycle Manager

cards.statement: AWS Backup can automatically run built-in application health checks during restore testing validation.
cards.explanation: A completed AWS Backup restore test restores the resource. Engineers supply application validation, such as a health check, through a separate workflow and report its result.
cards.misconception: AWS Backup supplies application-specific validation checks as part of restore testing.

source.title: Restore testing validation

cards.statement: AWS Lambda keeps existing unsigned ZIP code running after engineers attach an Enforce code signing configuration.
cards.explanation: AWS Lambda applies code signing checks to new code deployments. Attaching an Enforce configuration leaves the function's existing unsigned code running.

source.title: Creating code signing configurations for Lambda

cards.statement: A client can verify an Amazon S3 multipart upload by comparing its ETag with the MD5 digest of the entire object.
cards.explanation: For multipart uploads, Amazon S3's ETag is not the whole object's MD5 digest. Comparing it with a locally computed whole-file MD5 misidentifies valid uploads as corrupted.
cards.misconception: The ETag of a multipart object is its complete content's MD5 digest.

source.title: Object
